_about: Physical data for the Solar System page. Planets, Moon and Pluto: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (metric), D. R. Williams, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/ . Sun: NASA Sun Fact Sheet, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/sunfact.html , and IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal values. Ceres: Dawn mission results (Park et al. 2016, Nature 537, 515; Russell et al. 2016, Science 353, 1008) and NASA Science 'Ceres' pages. Spin-axis directions: IAU Working Group on Cartographic Coordinates and Rotational Elements (Archinal et al. 2018, Celest. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 130:22). Moon counts: NASA Science planet pages, as of 2025. Mean temperature for the giant planets is at the 1 bar pressure level (Fact Sheet convention). Negative rotation period = retrograde spin.

sources.label: Standish, Keplerian Elements for Approximate Positions of the Major Planets (JPL)
Archinal et al. 2018, IAU WGCCRE report (spin axes)

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.fact: Holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.temp_note: swings from about 430 °C by day to -180 °C at night
bodies.fact: Spins three times for every two orbits, so one solar day lasts two Mercury years.
missions: BepiColombo (ESA and JAXA; flybys 2021 to 2025, orbit arrival November 2026)

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.fact: Spins backwards, and so slowly that its day is longer than its year.

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.fact: The only world known to have liquid water on its surface and life.
missions: Home to every mission. Thousands of satellites orbit it today.

bodies.name: Moon
bodies.temp_note: from about 120 °C by day to -170 °C at night
bodies.fact: Tidally locked: the same face always points at Earth. It drifts away by about 3.8 cm per year.
missions: Apollo 11 to 17 (12 people walked on it, 1969 to 1972)

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.fact: Home to Olympus Mons, a volcano about 22 km high, and Valles Marineris, a canyon as long as the United States is wide.

bodies.name: Ceres
bodies.temp_note: about 168 K, estimated average surface temperature
bodies.fact: The largest object in the asteroid belt, between a quarter and a third of the belt's total mass. Its bright spots in Occator crater are salt deposits.

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.fact: More than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.fact: Less dense than water. Its main rings span about 270,000 km edge to edge, yet are typically only about 10 m thick.
missions: Cassini-Huygens (orbiter 2004 to 2017; Huygens landed on Titan 2005)

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.fact: Rolls around the Sun on its side: its axis is tilted 97.8 degrees, so each pole gets 42 years of sunlight then 42 of darkness.
bodies.moons_note: 28 on the Fact Sheet; S/2025 U1 announced by NASA in August 2025
missions: Voyager 2 (flyby, January 1986): the only visit so far

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.fact: Found in 1846 by mathematics before telescopes: Le Verrier predicted its position from wobbles in Uranus's orbit. Winds reach about 2,000 km/h.
missions: Voyager 2 (flyby, August 1989): the only visit so far

bodies.name: Pluto
bodies.fact: Its heart-shaped Sputnik Planitia is a glacier of nitrogen ice. Charon is so large that the pair orbit a point in space between them.

spacecraft._about: APPROXIMATE positions, for illustration only. Heliocentric distance on 2026-01-01 and radial speed are rounded from the NASA/JPL Voyager status page and New Horizons mission updates (Voyager 1: heliopause at 121.6 AU in August 2012, about 17.0 km/s; Voyager 2: heliopause at 119.0 AU in November 2018, about 15.4 km/s; New Horizons: 50 AU on 2021-04-17, about 13.7 km/s). Directions are rounded ecliptic longitude/latitude (J2000) derived from their catalogued right ascension and declination. The page draws a straight line from the last planetary flyby to the extrapolated position; the real paths curve slightly.

craft.name: Voyager 1
craft.note: Farthest human-made object. In interstellar space since August 2012.

craft.name: Voyager 2
craft.note: The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune. In interstellar space since November 2018.

craft.name: New Horizons
craft.note: Flew past Pluto in 2015 and Kuiper belt object Arrokoth on 1 January 2019.
